boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Johnsonville record (November 4-5, 1864) in the Franklin-Nashville Campaign [September-December 1864]. It closes Forrest's October 16-November 10 raid on the Tennessee River; the captures of October 29-30 at Fort Heiman and Paris Landing are outside the record. Campaign-wide marches, returns, reinforcements and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force text reads a supply depot garrison of approx. 4,000 against Forrest's cavalry; the live field reads 4,000 (US 4,000; CS 0). Sinclair lists the November 4 force as the 43d Wisconsin, 700 men, detachments of three colored regiments (number blank in print), 800 armed quartermaster's employees, 20 cavalry, three batteries and three gunboats. He reports Thompson's estimate of 13,000 Confederates with 36 guns and thinks it too large. Forrest describes the place as garrisoned by 'a heavy force' and the Union fire as coming from 28 guns on the gunboats and 14 on the hill.
claims.rationale: Sinclair's list is incomplete and its employees are not soldiers; Thompson's 13,000 is a scouting estimate. No figure for Forrest's own force was inspected. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: Sinclair says the river at Johnsonville is about 400 yards wide and straight, that hills come within 100 yards of the right bank, and that the left bank was flat and heavily wooded, uncleared before the attack. Forrest says the Union fort stood on a high hill with strong works and that his men built their batteries behind ambuscades that hid them. NPS says the Confederate guns were so well positioned the Federals could not hinder them.
claims.rationale: The river and wooded bank predate the action; the concealed batteries were built during it. Narrative descriptions.

claims.value: Johnsonville was the western terminus of the Nashville and Northwestern Railroad. Forrest on November 3 describes the landing and banks, several acres, piled with freight for Sherman's army, boats unloaded for want of room and trains running day and night, and says he had only his ordnance train and a few wagons. Sinclair says the property on the boats should have been landed between October 30 and November 4.
claims.rationale: Descriptions of the depot's stores and transport; no quartermaster return inspected.

claims.value: Sinclair says Colonel Thompson commanded the troops and Lieutenant-Commander King the gunboats; that King ordered the disabled gunboats abandoned and burned; that Thompson, on the recommendation of King, the gunboat officers and Howland, directed Howland to burn the transports; and that Thompson and Howland are responsible for the destruction. Forrest says he ordered the simultaneous opening at 3 o'clock. The frozen commanders are Major General Forrest (CS), Colonel C.R. Thompson and Lieutenant Commander Edward M. King (US); the live page lists 'Henry Thompson' and Sinclair prints 'Col. C. E. Thompson'.
claims.rationale: Sinclair's responsibility finding is an inspector's post-event judgment. The live name and Sinclair's initials are not adopted. No listed commander receives automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Confederate victory. Forrest says the wharf was a sheet of flame for nearly a mile by night and that he withdrew having completed the work of the expedition; Sinclair says the Confederates shelled the depot on the morning of the 5th and then left the river.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

claims.value: Forrest says his batteries set the gunboats on fire within fifteen minutes and then set the transports in flames. Sinclair says the gunboats were burned on King's order and the transports on Thompson's direction, that the firing of the boats was premature, and that the fire spread from them to the stores on the levee. NPS says the Federals set fire to the transports for fear of capture.
claims.rationale: The accounts conflict on who fired the boats; the conflict is preserved and not resolved.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads Unknown; the live field reads zeros. Sinclair gives the Union loss as 8 killed and wounded and the property destroyed or captured on the river as about $2,200,000 (NPS: $2.2 million). Forrest gives his loss for the whole expedition as 2 killed and 9 wounded, the enemy's as probably 500 killed, wounded and prisoners, and $6,700,000 worth of property.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Forrest's and Sinclair's property figures cover the whole river operation of October 28-November 5, not only this record.

open_questions: King's naval report (No. 5; printed with the army reports, not selected), the Navy reports cited by the compiler, Thomas's No. 1 dispatches and McConnell's No. 4 investigation (read, not selected), Donaldson's No. 3 report, Chalmers's No. 10 report and Cox's Johnsonville passage (pp.15–16, whose footnote gives the garrison as about 1,000; read, not selected) remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Jacob D. Cox's The March to the Sea; Franklin and Nashville (1882) is an interested history by the commander of the Twenty-third Corps' Third Division (and, at Franklin, of both divisions of that corps) that draws on official papers. Corse's, French's, R. S. Granger's, Doolittle's, Sinclair's, Forrest's, Hood's and Rousseau's reports, printed in Official Records Series I, Volumes XXXIX part 1 and XLV part 1, are separate families of interested accounts; each volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
